summary: This document defines an RTCP Extended Report block that reports burst and gap discard metrics, for use in a range of RTP applications.

eli5.summary: This tells whether thrown-away packets came in clumps or scattered one at a time.

questions: what is rtcp xr burst gap discard
what is gmin in rtcp xr
burst discard rate vs gap discard rate
subtitle: An RTCP report block that shows whether discarded packets came in clumps or were spread out.

tldr.problem: A total count of discarded packets does not show whether they were scattered or bunched together, and bunched discards hurt users much more.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7003 defines an RTCP Extended Report block (block type 20) with a 16-byte layout. It reports a burst threshold, the packets discarded in bursts and the total packets expected in bursts.
tldr.outcome: Combined with the total from RFC 7002, receivers of the report can work out burst and gap discard rates. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 7003 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2013, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It depends on RFC 7002 for the total discard count.

sections.title: Why Burstiness Matters
sections.content:
RFC 7003 adds a block to the RTCP Extended Report (XR) framework of RFC 3611. It reports the proportion of packets discarded by the receiver's jitter buffer, using the packet discard logic of the jitter buffer algorithm. It reports the discards that fall inside discard bursts together with the extent of those bursts.

The block gives information on transient IP problems. The burstiness of discards affects user experience, may influence any sender strategies to mitigate the problem, and may have diagnostic value. Burst/gap metrics are typically used in cumulative reports but may also be used in interval reports.

The block is intended to be used with RFC 7002, which provides the total packets discarded and on which this block therefore depends. The RFC 7002 metric can be used on its own, though. Reporting the actual jitter buffer algorithms is out of scope.
sections.eli5: It is not just how many packets got binned but whether they got binned in a big pile all at once.

sections.title: Discards, Bursts and Gaps
sections.content:
A packet is lost if it does not arrive within an implementation-specific time window. A packet that arrives in the window but is too early, too late or thrown away because of duplication or redundancy is discarded. A packet dropped later by a higher-layer decoder is not counted as discarded.

RTCP XR views a stream as divided into bursts, periods in which the discard rate is high enough to cause noticeable quality degradation (generally over 5 percent), and gaps, periods in which discards are infrequent and quality is generally acceptable. The method of telling them apart must be equivalent to the one in Section 4.7.2 of RFC 3611.

The block is aimed at RTP applications with de-jitter buffers that do not use stream repair such as forward error correction or retransmission.
sections.eli5: A burst is a rough patch where many packets get binned close together. A gap is a calm stretch where only the odd one goes.

sections.title: Measurement and Placement
sections.content:
Measurements are made at the receiving end of the RTP stream and refer to one stream by its SSRC. As in RFC 7002, the block depends on the Measurement Information Block of RFC 6776 for the span of the report.

Senders MUST send this block in the same compound RTCP packet as the Measurement Information Block. Receivers MUST verify that the measurement period arrived in the same compound packet and MUST discard the block if it did not.
sections.eli5: The score sheet must come in the same envelope as the note saying which match it is for.

sections.title: The Burst/Gap Discard Metrics Block
sections.content:
The block is BT=20 with a Block Length of 3 (MUST; any other value means the block MUST be discarded). The first word holds the 8-bit block type, the 2-bit Interval Metric flag, 6 reserved bits and the 16-bit length. Then come the 32-bit SSRC of Source and two more words.

  • Threshold (8 bits): equivalent to Gmin in RFC 3611, the number of successive packets that must not be discarded before and after a discarded packet for it to count as part of a gap.
  • Packets Discarded in Bursts (24 bits): total packets discarded during discard bursts.
  • Total Packets Expected in Bursts (24 bits): the sum of received and lost packets during bursts.
  • A final 8-bit reserved field.

The I flag works as in RFC 7002: I=10 is an interval value and I=11 is cumulative. Senders MUST NOT use I=00 or I=01, and receivers MUST discard blocks that carry them. Reserved bits MUST be zero on send and are ignored on receipt.

For the two 24-bit counts, a value above 0xFFFFFD is reported as 0xFFFFFE (over-range), and 0xFFFFFF means the measurement is unavailable.
sections.eli5: The form has a box for how picky to be about what counts as a rough patch, a box for packets binned in rough patches, and a box for how many were due in rough patches.

sections.title: Derived Metrics and VoIP
sections.content:
The block is meant to be read with the Measurement Information Block and with the discard count from RFC 7002. From the two burst figures a receiver of the report can calculate the fraction of packets discarded during bursts (the Burst Discard Rate in RFC 7004), and the matching gap discard rate. RFC 7004 describes the calculations in detail.

For Voice-over-IP with no stream repair, a call is viewed as bursts of noticeable degradation (generally over 5 percent discard) and gaps of acceptable quality. If voice activity detection is used, burst and gap durations are determined as if silence packets had been sent, so a silence longer than Gmin packets ends a burst. The recommended Gmin from RFC 3611 makes a burst similar to a typical pulse code modulation severely errored second.
sections.eli5: From the pile counts you can work out what share of packets were binned in rough patches and what share in calm stretches.

sections.title: Signaling With SDP
sections.content: The block can be announced with the SDP rtcp-xr attribute from RFC 3611. RFC 7003 adds the xr-format value burst-gap-discard. The offer/answer rules for unilateral rtcp-xr parameters in RFC 3611 apply, and XR blocks MAY also be used without prior signaling.
sections.eli5: You can tell the other side in advance that you will send this report, but you may also just send it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC believes this block adds no new security considerations beyond those in RFC 3611. Because it carries no per-packet statistics, the confidentiality risk documented in RFC 3611 does not apply.
sections.eli5: The report only gives totals, not details about each packet, so it gives away very little.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC assigns block type 20 to the Burst/Gap Discard Metrics Block in the IANA RTCP XR Block Type Registry. It also registers the SDP parameter burst-gap-discard. Appendix A restates the three metrics (threshold, packets discarded in bursts and total packets expected in bursts) using the template from RFC 6390.
sections.eli5: The block gets its own official number and name so everyone agrees what it is.

fields.name: SSRC of Source
fields.desc: The stream the report is about.

fields.name: Total Packets Expected in Bursts
fields.desc: Received plus lost packets during bursts.
